messages.subject: Web based sampling and demography
messages.body_plain:
Here is a question i hope someone may have some insights for me.

I am in the process of starting up a long-term project that involves
rodent demography. I switched from a grid-based to web-based after
reading Parmenter et al 2003 (Ecol Mono.). Now, I am wondering about
estimating demographic parameters (e.g, surviorship).

The current design is as follows:
1. Web-based design (10 traps at 10m spacing with 12 radial lines, with
4 traps at the center of the web = 124 traps total). I have been running
the grids for 5 consective nights, marking each individual animal.

2. The grids are being sampled between 3-5 times a year.

Can I use MARK (e.g, CJS, Prandel) to estimate demographic parameters
with this web-based design, or would that violate any assumptions (i.e.,
each marked animal has the equal probablility of being recaptured)?

THE BIG QUESTION BEING: If i am interested in demographic parameters
(particularly in a comparative sense between certain grids), as well as
density - is it better to use a grid-based or web-based design?

any insights would be excellent. thanks!

cheers,
josh

messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am analyzing data from a project that examined the differences in avian
densities between native (>2/3 native) and non-native habitat (<1/3
native).  We surveyed avian communities over three years with the use of
point transects.  I used distance sampling and stratified by habitat to get
a density for each habitat.

  I'm trying to determine if I can use distance sampling for another aspect
of the project.  There is variation in the percentage of native and
non-native habitat at each point so we also collected vegetation data
corresponding to each point.  I would like to examine avian density at
different percentages of native and non-native habitat.  The problem is
that I do not have enough data to stratify by points.  Can I apply the
detection probability from the habitats (native and non-native) to the
corresponding individual points that fall in those categories to get
densities for individual points?  I apologize ahead of time if this is a
ridiculous question, but I'm new to distance sampling and I'm trying to
explore its different applications.

Cheers,
Kristina

messages.body_plain:
Further to Jeff's reply:

> >A) How can I export (and into which program?) the detection function
> >graph? Is it possible to construct it in Excel or Adobe Illustrator?

Jeff's answer is quite correct, and you could have saved him the trouble of
answering you by pressing F1 in Distance, and then looking in the online help
index under "Copy | Results to other programs".

In addition, if you had searched the online archives of the distance-sampling
list (available from within Distance by choosing "Help | Distance on the web |
distance-sampling list archive", using the key words "plot" or "Excel" with the
substring search button ticked, you would have found the message titled
"ANNOUNCE: Excel macro for Distance g(x) plots".  This macro (written by Tim
Gerrodette) takes the numbers produced when you paste a plot into excel using
"paste" rather than "paste special" and turns them back into a plot which you
can then customize.  The macro is available from the "Distance Support, Updates
and Extras" page of the Distance web site.  It was originally written for
Distance 3.5, but I expect it will work fine for Distance 4 plots too (although
I haven't tried it).  If it doesn't work please contact me and I'll fix it up.

My general point here is please check all available sources of information
before posting to the list.

> >B) As I am using Whitesides (1987?) method of establishing the
> >perpendicular distance to the center of the primate group - by
> >incorporating average group spread and adding 1/2 of that to the
> >perpendicular distance measured from line to the first primate - there
> >is a new source of error which is added(=group spread). (I understand
> >that the method has some draw backs, however it proved most practical
> >in dense vegetation.) HOW can I incorporate the variation and its
> >standard error in DISTANCE. I have been trying to add it as a
> >multiplier, but I have not managed to keep track of the analysis in
> >that way and so feel unsure about the results.

Aha - now this was a valid question!  Again Dr Distance (Jeff) was quite right
that it's a measurement error and can't be addressed directly in Distance.  The
only solution I can think of if you have access to someone who can program is to
write a little simulation program that creates samples from your original data
like a regular bootstrap but also adding in the measurement error (i.e., adding
in random values drawn from the distribution of group spread), runs Distance
from the command line (see online help about this) and extracts the results --
repeat this many times to incorporate the uncertainty in distances.

We have a student here, Tiago Marques, who is interested in measurement error,
so I'm cc'ing this to him to see if he can think of anything more practical
(he's away for much of the summer so it will likely be a while before you hear
from him).

One approach would be to guesstimate how big the effect of such measurement
errors might be.  One way to categorize measurement error is as either additive
(the error is added to the true distances) or multiplicative (the error
multiplies or divides the true distance).  I haven't read the Whiteside paper
you refer to, but from what you said it seems you have additive errors -- you
add in 1/2 the group spread estimate.  There's a paper by Song Chen (1998) in
Biometrics that looks at additive errors, with some results summarized on page
264 of Introduction to Distance sampling: "Chen (1998) showed that the expected
bias was a function of the error magnitude and the width of the shoulder of the
detection function (i.e. values of x such that g(x) is approximately 1).  When
the standard deviation of the measurement errors was approximately one-half the
width of the detection function shoulder, the expected bias in density was less
than -3%."  This addresses any possible bias caused by the measurement error; I
don't remember if Song also looked at the increase in variance caused by the
additional source of uncertainty.

Hope this helps a little!

 - Len

--

messages.body_plain:
Kristina,

Here's a suggestion, but not a definative answer -- others may have other
suggestions/ideas:

You could use %native as a covariate in a multiple covariate analysis (MCDS
analysis engine).  This allows the scale of the detection function to vary as %
native varies.  Then predict density for each point (under Model Definition |
Estimate tick the Density by sample box).  Get these predicted densities out of
Distance and into some other stats package, and do a regression of estimated
density against percentage of native habitat at each point.  Since density is
(at least close to) log-normally distributed (Introduction to Distance page 77)
you may want to log-transform the densities before doing the regression -- you
can then assume errors are normally distributed.  As a refinement, you could
weight each density by its estimated CV if they are very different between
points (unlikely).

For getting the density estimates out of distance, you could do it manually
(i.e., type the estimates into a stats package) or if you have the skill you
could write a little program to parse the stats file that Distance can output
with each run (look in the online help Index under "Saving CDS analysis results
| Saving to file").

By the way, can I remind people to use appropriate subject lines when they post
to the list -- we've had two postings in one day with no subject line - this
makes it hard for people to follow up any replies and find messages in the
archive.  A suggested subject for this post might be "Question: differences
between habitats".  For more on this, see point 2 of the list guidelines at
http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/files/DISTANCE-SAMPLING/distance-sampling.welcome

Cheers,

 - Len

messages.subject: data truncation??
messages.body_plain:
Greetings, I have a dataset collected from Mexico on a small, insectivorous
bird.  Data were collected from points laid out at least 250 m from one
another in a systematic grid across relatively homogeneous habitat.  Fifty
points were surveyed yielding 142 registrations.  Actual distances were
recorded using a laser rangefinder.  Distances recorded ranged from 1 to 100
m, the latter record being the sole observation beyond 60 m.  Every effort
was made to record data at, or near, the point (r=0) in each case.  However,
upon inspecting a histogram of the data it is clear that much heaping occurs
around the 40 m mark, with none at the points (r=0) and very few within
about r=20 m.  I have been attempting several truncation approaches to
minimize bias, including:

right-truncate beyond 60, no left truncation
right-truncate the greatest 10% (as suggested by Buckland et al. 2001:151),
no left truncation
right-truncate beyond 60, left truncate within 20 m (chosen more or less
arbitrarily but in light of the fact that very few records exist in that
group)
right-truncate the greatest 10%, left truncate within 20 m

AIC values (587-507) seem to go down with increasing truncation effort, but
density (3.7-4.5) and cv (9.8%-11.6%) increase slightly.  I am wondering how
significant these truncation efforts are in yielding the most robust model
estimates of density.  Additionally, I have tried several types of cutpoint
intervals, but all around 10 groupings each with little change in AIC,
density and cv values.

Is there anything else I should try?

Craig Farquhar, PhD
Avian Ecologist
Wildlife Diversity Branch
Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
3000 S IH-35, Ste. 100
Austin, Texas  78704
work tel:  512-912-7018
work fax:  512-912-7058
email:   <mailto:craig.f...@tpwd.state.tx.us>

messages.subject: Re: data truncation??
messages.body_plain:
> > AIC values (587-507) seem to go down with increasing truncation effort, but
> > density (3.7-4.5) and cv (9.8%-11.6%) increase slightly.  I am wondering how
> > significant these truncation efforts are in yielding the most robust model
> > estimates of density.  Additionally, I have tried several types of cutpoint
> > intervals, but all around 10 groupings each with little change in AIC,
> > density and cv values.

Craig, as noted in the 1993 and 2001 books, 'AIC can only be used to
compare models fitted to exactly the same data.  It cannot therefore be
used to select a truncation distance w, or to compare models if different
truncation distances have been used, or to assess whether, or how, to
group distance data.' (p 111 of the 2001 book.)

If you're using a laser rangefinder, it seems unlikely that you have any
significant heaping, and more likely that you are mis-interpreting your
data.  For point transect sampling, there is almost no area within say 2
metres of a point, so you expect no, or almost no, detections.  There is
much more area between say 39m and 41m (40 times as much area), so
you get more detections at around 40m.  At greater distances, you fail to
detect many birds, so numbers fall again.  Hence your histogram should
increase then decrease.  If you select the point transect option in
Distance, its fits will also have this property.  If goodness-of-fit
suggests you still have too few detections near the point and too many at
40m, this may be because birds are moving away from the observer before
being detected.

Right-truncation at around 60m would probably be OK for your data.  I
would not left-truncate unless I was convinced there really was a serious
problem with the reliability of small distances.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: data truncation??
messages.body_plain:
Hi Craig, List,

The pattern you describe (very little data close to the point, a hump at some
distance out and then little data at greater distances) is exactly what one
expects for point transect data -- see, for example Buckland et al 2001 figures
5.1 and 5.2.  This is because two things are going on at once: the detection
probability decreases as you move away from the point in a non-linear fashion,
but the area surveyed  (see figure 2.3) increases linearly.  I put an overhead
from our introductory workshop on the web which will hopefully make this clear -
see http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/points.pdf

It's hard to give specific advice about truncation without seeing the data, and
I'm wary of cookbook recipes -- but truncation of around 10% of point transect
data is a good starting point.  The aim is to remove "outliers" -- that is the
odd observation at large distances that can cause Distance to add an extra
adjustment term when it doesn't affect the fit at 0 distance and only decreases
precision.  As a rough gude, and assuming "good" data, try fitting any old
detection function and truncating 10%; if there are one or more adjustment terms
fit, try a slightly greater truncation and see if you can get it to drop one of
the adjustment terms, and if it does, see if it makes the estimate of h(0) more
precise.  Not something to get hung up about though -- with "good" data it
should make little difference for truncations of about this much -- i.e., the
density estimate should not move much relative to its standard error, and the CV
should not change greatly.

Note that you cannot compare AIC amoung analyses with different truncations (or
cutpoints, when intervals are specified in the Data Filter).  AIC is only a
valid comparison when you're comparing analyses using exactly the same input
data, and truncation changes the data.

I would avoid left truncation, especially for point transect data where the
observations made close to the point are especially important in determining the
slope of f(x) at 0 distance -- which is the h(0) in equation 3.14 of the book.
You can use the goodness-of-fit tests to check whether there really is a serious
lack of fit of the data close to the point.

I would also avoid putting the data into intervals for the analysis, especially
since you collected exact distances with a laser rangefinder.  When the data are
"good" all you do by putting data into intervals is loose some precision --
although it usually makes little difference in practice when you get about 7 or
more intervals.  I *would* recommend specifying your own cutpoints for the
diagnostic goodness-of-fit tests (under Model Definition | Detection function |
Diagnostics) but this is only for the gof tests and not for fitting the
detection function, so makes no difference to the acutal fit (there's lots more
about this point in the online manual).

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Multi-species sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hello-
I am conducting surveys of birds in urban parks using line transects.  I am
particularly interested in guild composition in the parks, as the parks
vary considerably in amount of forest habitat, density of both overstory
and understory, amount of shrub habitat, etc. as well as in area.  I was
hoping to compare composition and density for several guilds across parks
by summing individual species=92 density estimates within a guild, for
example, ground nesters, in each park.  However, for several species, our
sample sizes are too small to obtain reliable species-level density
estimates.  I am wondering about calculating densities for multiple species
within a guild, as indicated in the 2001 book on page 301-302.  Could I
group several species with similar detectabilities that occur in the same
guild and calculate an overall density estimate for the group?  What should
I do if some species are absent from that guild in some of the parks (due
to area or habitat patch size, for example)?  Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
> > I am conducting surveys of birds in urban parks using line transects.  I =

am
> > particularly interested in guild composition in the parks, as the parks
> > vary considerably in amount of forest habitat, density of both overstory
> > and understory, amount of shrub habitat, etc. as well as in area.  I was
> > hoping to compare composition and density for several guilds across parks
> > by summing individual species=92 density estimates within a guild, for
> > example, ground nesters, in each park.  However, for several species, our
> > sample sizes are too small to obtain reliable species-level density

> > estimates.  I am wondering about calculating densities for multiple speci=

es
> > within a guild, as indicated in the 2001 book on page 301-302.  Could I
> > group several species with similar detectabilities that occur in the same

> > guild and calculate an overall density estimate for the group?  What shou=

ld
> > I do if some species are absent from that guild in some of the parks (due
> > to area or habitat patch size, for example)?  Thanks!

Yes, if you pool across species, you should still get a valid estimate of
overall density - provided each individual species satisfies the
assumptions of line transect sampling.  Differences in detectability
between species do not invalidate this overall density estimate, but they
DO generate bias in density estimates by species, if you assume a common
detection function - more detectable species will be overestimated, and
less detectable species underestimated.  I'm not sure why it should be a
problem if some species from within a guild are absent from some parks.
They clearly contribute zero density in those parks - both in terms of
true density and in terms of estimated density.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: chiroptera
messages.body_plain:
> > I am going to begin to work in the estimation of the
> > abundance and density of urban bats in my city.
> > I am going to look for roots with the point sampling
> > and to use the program of Distance 4.

If you plan to record flying bats from points, that will not work if the
aim is to estimate absolute abundance, because point transect sampling
seriously overestimates abundance if the animals are moving around to the
extent that flying bats do.  To avoid this, you need to be able to take a
'snapshot' from each point (see 2001 distance sampling book).  I'm not
sure if this will be feasible in your study.  (Sample size can be enhanced
by taking a series of snapshots at each point, perhaps with a few minutes
between each.  The distances to each bat at each snapshot moment can then
be pooled, and effort at the point recorded as the number of snapshot
moments at that point.

If these methods are not workable, you may have to just resort to a
relative index of abundance.  Often for bats, bat 'passes' are counted,
using bat detectors.  In this case, it is often difficult or impossible to
get distance data, and to determine how many different bats were detected.
Also, snapshot methods don't work well when relying on bat detectors.
Bat detectors do allow identification of species, which can be problematic
for visual detections.

If anyone has developed reliable line or point transect methods for bats,
I would be interested to hear, as these seem a particularly difficult
group of species!

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: Group spread CV
messages.body_plain:
> > The second question I had put forward was as following:
> > I measured the perpendicular distance from line transect to the first

> > primate sighted. Following Whitesides et al. (1988) I added half of

> > the estimated group spread for the observed primate species to the

> > perpendicular distance. My question was how to incorporate the error,

> > which is induced with this method onto DISTANCE. You mentioned that

> > this is not possible directly because it is a measurement error.

> > However group spread itself is not a measurement error to he

> > perpendicular distance. For example group spread for Blue monkeys has

> > a mean of =65.7m (n=3163, CV=1.0%) If I use this mean and add half of

> > it to the perpendicular distance I induce a potential variable which I

> > need to account for in the analysis? Is it still not possible to

> > include as a multiplier?

I can't see any sensible way to add it as a multiplier, since you want an
additive effective, not a multiplicative one.  (Distance groups are not
expected to have greater spreads than near ones.)  Adding half the spread
to recorded perpendicular distance to the nearest animal (to the line) of
the group is OK, except for groups that span the line, for which you will
need a different procedure to identify the location of the centre of the
group.  If you want to allow for uncertainty in centre location, you could
use the bootstrap:  in the above case, you could resample values from say
a normal distribution with mean 65.7/2 and std error sqrt(3163)*(0.657/2).
However, this could not be done within Distance.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: weighting global density estimate in model definition properties
messages.subject_clean: weighting global density estimate in model definition properties
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance list subscribers,

I'd like to ask for some help with Distance 4 release 2. FYI, all
observations were collected as exact distances perpendicular from the line.
I suspect my detection function will differ between regions.

I have two geographic regions and would like to stratify via the stratum
data layer to get density estimates for both. In the "Model Definition
Properties" "Estimate" tab, I am unclear how to weight my global density
estimate. My area for each region is zero (from the area field in the data
explorer). The F1 help menu says to use the default settings for geographic
stratification, but there is no picture so I am unsure as to what weighting
is appropriate. Weighting by area gives a higher density estimate than
giving equal weighting to all strata, even though the area is set to zero.
My gut feeling is that I should give equal weight to all strata, because I
have eight transects of equal length in each region.

As always, thanks in advance for any help you can give.

Sincerely,
Joe Roberts
Graduate Student
Dept. of Zoology
Univ. of Oklahoma

messages.body_plain:
> > I have two geographic regions and would like to stratify via the stratum
> > data layer to get density estimates for both. In the "Model Definition
> > Properties" "Estimate" tab, I am unclear how to weight my global density
> > estimate. My area for each region is zero (from the area field in the data
> > explorer). The F1 help menu says to use the default settings for geographic
> > stratification, but there is no picture so I am unsure as to what weighting
> > is appropriate. Weighting by area gives a higher density estimate than
> > giving equal weighting to all strata, even though the area is set to zero.
> > My gut feeling is that I should give equal weight to all strata, because I
> > have eight transects of equal length in each region.

As Len is on holiday, I'll respond briefly - as I'm not sure what Distance
does in this circumstance, he might clarify once he is back.

First, I'm puzzled why you have set your areas to zero.  Second, if you
want global density, it should be

(total number of animals in popn)/(total area)

The number of transects you have in each stratum has nothing to do with
this.  But you can only get a valid estimate of this density if you have
transects randomly positioned in each stratum (or a randomly-positioned
grid of transects).  The no. (and length) of transects in each stratum
affects precision, but not weighting.

When strata are geographic, you get the global density by taking a
weighted average of stratum densities, where weights are stratum
areas.  If you don't give any stratum areas, I'm not sure what the default
is - I would have guessed it is to weight by total effort in each stratum,
which is fine provided line length per stratum is proportional to stratum
size.  In your case, this should be the same as giving equal weighting to
each stratum estimate, but your results show it is not doing that.  Note
that, for geographic strata, you must take the global density estimate as
the mean, not the sum, of the stratum estimates - I assume you're doing
that?

The simple solution is to give Distance the appropriate stratum areas -
and if you can't, it is because you don't have well-defined geographic
strata, so that a global density is not well-defined.  In that case, I
would just get the stratum density estimates, and not seek to get a global
estimate.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Dear All, forgive me if this is a novice's question, but I am a novice.
If I have 82 observations of zebra in plains habitat, and 4 observations
in Acacia habitat, and have specified the area for both, why does DISTANCE
report a value for N (which I understand to be abundance) as zero, when I
recorded a total of over 500 animals in the area.  Also based on minimum
AIC the model selected for plains habitat was negative exponential even
though p = 1.000 for the transect, surely the uniform model would have
been more appropriate.  Many thanks justine Shelley
